questions.q: What is the difference between a compatibility issue and a feature parity gap, per this lesson?
options: Both terms only apply to network configuration, never to database features
A compatibility issue actively breaks and blocks the migration until fixed; a feature parity gap doesn't block the migration but the capability doesn't exist on the target
A feature parity gap always prevents a migration from completing, while a compatibility issue never does
They are the same thing described with two different names
questions.explain: Compatibility issues block the migration; parity gaps mean the migration succeeds but a capability behaves differently or is missing.

questions.q: Which example does this lesson give of a feature parity gap rather than a compatibility issue?
options: A missing backup file
A syntax error that prevents the migration tool from running at all
An expired SQL Server license
Cross-database queries and linked servers not existing in Azure SQL Database
questions.explain: The database migrates fine to Azure SQL Database; it's the specific cross-database capability that doesn't come with it — a parity gap, not a blocker.

questions.q: What three inputs does this lesson identify as driving a real sizing/tier recommendation?
options: Peak CPU/memory utilization, storage size and growth trend, and IOPS/throughput requirements
Only the SQL Server version currently installed
Only the total number of tables in the database
The DBA's personal preference and the vendor's marketing tier names
questions.explain: These three measured inputs turn into a real vCore/DTU tier recommendation, rather than guessing.

questions.q: Why does this lesson specify peak CPU/memory rather than average utilization for sizing?
options: Because Azure only accepts average values as valid input
Because average and peak are always identical in practice
Because average utilization hides the actual bottleneck moment that a tier choice needs to handle
Because peak values are always lower than average values
questions.explain: Sizing for the bottleneck moment (peak), not the typical moment (average), avoids under-provisioning for real load.

questions.q: What does this lesson say happens if compatibility and parity assessment is skipped before migration?
options: Issues get discovered during the actual cutover, the worst possible time, instead of as a known list beforehand
Azure automatically performs the assessment for free with zero DBA involvement
The migration automatically fails safely with no downtime impact
Nothing changes — assessment has no real effect on migration outcomes
questions.explain: Assessment turns unknown risks into a known, addressed list before any downtime window starts.
